subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Data and Graphing Reading
subtitle: Reading practice on data, graph choice, fair tests, outliers, and engineering evidence.
description: Students practise identifying variables, choosing graph types, reading scales and units, and using data as evidence. The pack emphasizes fair tests, patterns, outliers, repeated trials, and Claim-Evidence-Reasoning for science and engineering decisions.

data.sourcePassage: A student might think one paper towel is best because it looks thicker, but science needs stronger evidence than appearance alone. A fair investigation would test different paper towel brands using the same towel size, the same water amount, the same soaking time, and the same draining method. The paper towel brand would be the independent variable. The amount of water absorbed, measured in milliliters, would be the dependent variable. Repeated trials would make the results more reliable. After recording the results in a table, the student could make a bar graph to compare brands. A strong claim would use specific data, such as one brand absorbing more milliliters of water than the others.

questions.question: What is the independent variable in the paper towel investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: The paper towel brand is the independent variable.

questions.question: What unit could be used to measure the water absorbed?
questions.modelAnswer: Milliliters could be used to measure the amount of water absorbed.

questions.question: Which graph type would usually be best for comparing paper towel brands?
questions.modelAnswer: A bar graph would compare the categories of paper towel brands.

questions.question: Why would repeated trials make the claim stronger?
questions.modelAnswer: Repeated trials help check reliability and reduce the effect of random variation or one unusual result.

questions.question: Why is saying “it looks thicker” weaker than using measured data?
questions.modelAnswer: Appearance is only an observation, while measured absorption data gives specific evidence that can be compared.

data.sourcePassage: Different graph types answer different kinds of questions. Bar graphs are useful when scientists compare categories, such as insulation materials or bridge designs. Line graphs are useful for continuous change, especially change over time, such as temperature measured every hour. Pie charts show parts of a whole, such as percentages of waste types in a cafeteria. Scatter plots show pairs of numerical data so scientists can look for relationships, such as height and arm span. Choosing the wrong graph can hide patterns or make data harder to interpret. A complete graph also needs a clear title, labeled axes, units, and an even scale.

data.sourcePassage: In a fair test, scientists change one main variable and keep other important conditions the same. For example, a class might ask how water temperature affects the time it takes a sugar cube to dissolve. The independent variable is water temperature because that is changed on purpose. The dependent variable is dissolving time because it is measured. Controlled variables should include the same amount of water, same sugar cube size, same stirring method, and same timer method. If the student changed both temperature and sugar cube size, it would be difficult to know which variable caused any change in dissolving time.

questions.question: Why is it a problem to change both temperature and sugar cube size?

questions.question: How does a fair test make evidence stronger?
questions.modelAnswer: It controls other explanations, so changes in the dependent variable are more likely linked to the independent variable.

data.sourcePassage: Scientists analyze data by looking for trends, relationships, and unusual results. A trend might show values increasing, decreasing, staying about the same, or repeating in a cycle. An outlier is a data point that is very different from the rest. In a dissolving test, times of 42 seconds, 44 seconds, and 15 seconds would make the 15-second result suspicious. Scientists should not automatically delete outliers. They should ask whether the water was hotter, the tablet was already broken, the timer was started late, or the result was unusual but real. Repeated trials help scientists decide whether results are reliable.

questions.question: What should scientists do before deleting an outlier?
questions.modelAnswer: They should investigate possible errors or unusual conditions and may repeat the test.

questions.question: Why do repeated trials help with reliability?
questions.modelAnswer: Repeated trials show whether results are consistent and reduce the effect of random variation.

questions.question: Why might an unusual result still matter scientifically?
questions.modelAnswer: It might reveal a real condition or pattern that scientists need to understand rather than ignore.

data.sourcePassage: Engineers use data to compare designs and improve solutions. In a paper bridge challenge, teams might be limited to three sheets of paper and 20 cm of tape. They can measure the mass each bridge holds before collapse. A flat strip might hold 120 g, a folded accordion might hold 410 g, rolled tubes might hold 530 g, and a triangle truss might hold 620 g. The triangle truss is strongest in this data set because it holds the most mass. A strong engineering explanation also includes reasoning: triangle shapes help spread forces through a structure. Engineers may still consider other data, such as build time, cost, stability, and comfort, before choosing a final design.
